definition: Servile means excessively submissive and eager to please.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word servile. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know servile should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The valet's servile murmur of agreement followed the baron from room to room like a draft.
Respectful is far milder than servile — a respectful junior lawyer lets the partner speak first and still argues her own view, while the servile junior has handed her opinions over entirely.
Groveling goes further than servile — the servile aide flatters and agrees, while the groveler throws dignity away outright, begging where he could simply ask.

Fawning is flattery poured out to win favor — the compliments come thick because the fawner wants something from the person above. Servile is bigger than flattery: the whole posture is excessively submissive, eager to please at the cost of one's own opinions and standing.

Obsequious points at the performance itself — oily, overdone deference, endless agreeing and anticipating of wishes, embarrassing to watch. Servile points at what that performance costs: a servile person has gone past courtesy into self-erasure, trading opinions and dignity for approval.

The commis chef tastes nothing until the head chef tastes first.
He asks permission to salt the water, thanks the head chef twice for every correction, and last week called his own knife work clumsy because the head chef frowned at an onion.
The kitchen has stopped expecting so servile a junior to have opinions.
Servile is the exact word for the commis, because servile means excessively submissive and eager to please — the excess is what the word faults.
Respectful keeps its footing: a respectful junior speaks politely and still says what she thinks; the servile one has handed his opinions over with his coat.
Servile is an accusation: submission has gone past courtesy into self-erasure.
Its unit-mates grade the slope — obedience does what it is told and keeps its dignity, docile is simply easy to lead, compliant just meets the rules.

Nobody on the campaign could say when Tomas stopped being an adviser and became an echo.
In the early months he had argued with the candidate daily, and his memos were famous for their red ink.
By spring, the red ink was gone.
He praised drafts he privately thought disastrous, agreed with positions that reversed his own published work, and once stood silent while the candidate misquoted him to his face.
Colleagues stopped asking his opinion, because his opinion was now whatever had just been said.
A rival aide put it cruelly but precisely: Tomas had become servile — not merely polite to power, but emptied out by it, his judgment traded piece by piece for a seat near the front of the plane.
